scenario: An early-stage employee of a tech startup was promised 2% equity through ESOP but upon funding round, the equity was diluted to 0.5% without proper notification. The employee challenged this dilution.
facts: The employee joined a pre-seed startup as employee #5. Verbal promise of 2% equity was made. ESOP grant letter stated 2% but did not mention anti-dilution provisions. After Series A funding, effective stake reduced to 0.5%.
legal_issues: Fiduciary duties of directors towards option holders
Rights of ESOP holders during funding rounds
judgment: The court held partially in favor of the employee. While dilution is normal in funding rounds, the company failed to: 1) Clearly communicate dilution provisions, 2) Provide anti-dilution protection as industry standard, 3) Act in good faith towards option holders. The court ordered the company to either: a) Provide additional options to restore effective ownership to 1.5%, or b) Allow employee to sell back options at fair market value with 50% premium.
key_principles: ESOP grant letters must clearly state dilution and vesting terms
Anti-dilution provisions for early employees are industry standard
Directors have fiduciary duty of good faith towards ESOP holders
Verbal promises backed by partial documentation can be enforced
Company must act fairly and transparently with employee stakeholders
SEBI regulations mandate proper ESOP disclosures
precedents: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd. (1981)
Securities and Exchange Board of India v. Shri Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel (2017)
Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya (1959) - Promissory Estoppel
practical_advice: Always get ESOP terms in writing, never rely on verbal promises
Understand vesting schedule (typically 4 years with 1-year cliff)
Check for anti-dilution provisions in ESOP agreement
Understand difference between percentage ownership vs. number of shares
Ask about company's valuation cap and expected dilution
Review ESOP grant letter with lawyer before accepting
Maintain all written communications about equity promises
Understand tax implications of ESOPs in India

scenario: A co-founder CTO was forced to resign by other founders due to personal conflicts. Upon resignation, the company refused to accelerate vesting of unvested shares, resulting in forfeiture of 60% of promised equity.
facts: The CTO co-founded the company with 25% equity subject to 4-year vesting with 1-year cliff. After 18 months, due to disagreements, other founders created hostile work environment forcing resignation. Founders' agreement had no acceleration clause for termination without cause.
legal_issues: Vesting acceleration in case of wrongful termination
Oppression and mismanagement under Companies Act
applicable_laws: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Breach of contract
judgment: The court ruled in favor of the CTO, holding that: 1) The resignation was constructive dismissal due to hostile environment, 2) Founders breached their fiduciary duties, 3) Forfeiture of equity in such circumstances amounts to oppression. The court ordered: a) Full acceleration of vesting for all unvested shares, b) Company to purchase shares at fair market value if CTO wishes to exit, c) Damages for mental harassment and loss of reputation.
key_principles: Constructive dismissal triggers same protections as wrongful termination
Co-founders owe fiduciary duties to each other
Oppression and mismanagement provisions protect minority shareholders
Vesting acceleration may be ordered in cases of bad faith termination
Founders' agreements must have clear dispute resolution mechanisms
Courts can order fair value buyout in founder disputes
precedents: Shanti Prasad Jain v. Kalinga Tubes Ltd. (1965) - Oppression
Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. v. Tata Sons Ltd. (2020) - Shareholder rights
Vodafone International Holdings v. Union of India (2012) - Shareholder agreements
practical_advice: Always have a detailed founders' agreement with vesting terms
Include acceleration clauses for termination without cause
Define 'good leaver' and 'bad leaver' scenarios clearly
Single trigger vs. double trigger acceleration - understand the difference
Document all founder decisions and disagreements
Consider having independent board members for founder disputes
Reverse vesting protects all founders equally
Include mediation/arbitration clauses in founders' agreement

case_name: Tech Company - Employee Moonlighting and Conflict of Interest
scenario: A senior engineer was discovered working for two tech companies simultaneously, dedicating full-time hours to both. The primary employer filed suit for breach of contract and recovery of paid wages.
facts: The engineer worked 9 AM to 6 PM for Company A and 7 PM to 2 AM for Company B (both remote positions). Both companies believed they had an exclusive full-time employee. Neither employment contract explicitly prohibited dual employment but had clauses requiring 'full dedication and loyalty'.
legal_issues: Dual employment and moonlighting in IT sector
Implied duty of loyalty and good faith
Conflict of interest in competing companies
applicable_laws: Shops and Establishments Act - Multiple employment restrictions
judgment: The court held in favor of the primary employer. Key findings: 1) Dual full-time employment amounts to fraud by misrepresentation, 2) Even without explicit prohibition, implied duty of loyalty was breached, 3) Working for competitor creates inherent conflict of interest, 4) Employee must return 50% of wages received as unjust enrichment. The court granted: a) Permanent injunction against working for competitor, b) Recovery of wages for period of dual employment, c) Damages for breach of loyalty.
key_principles: Employees have implied duty of loyalty towards employer
Dual full-time employment amounts to fraud and breach of contract
Moonlighting without disclosure is breach of good faith
Working for direct competitor creates conflict of interest
Unjust enrichment doctrine applies to wages earned through breach
Remote work doesn't change fundamental employment duties
precedents: Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan (2006) - Duty of loyalty
Niranjan Shankar Golikari v. Century Spinning (1967) - Employee obligations
Raman Tech. & Process Engg. Co. v. Solanki Traders (2008) - Good faith
practical_advice: Always disclose any dual employment or side work to primary employer
Check employment contract for moonlighting clauses
Remote work doesn't make dual employment acceptable
Working for competitors creates significant legal risks
Freelancing or consulting may be acceptable with disclosure
Some companies now allow moonlighting with restrictions - check policy
Maintain clear separation of work if moonlighting is permitted
Consider legal advice before taking on secondary employment

case_name: Startup Acquisition - Employee Rights and Retention
scenario: A tech startup was acquired by a larger company. Employees were promised retention bonuses and continued employment for 2 years. Six months post-acquisition, several employees were terminated without cause and denied retention bonuses.
facts: During acquisition, employees signed new contracts with 2-year retention clauses and significant retention bonuses payable on completion. Acquiring company restructured 6 months later, laying off 40% of acquired company's staff. Terminated employees sought retention bonuses and damages.
legal_issues: Transfer of undertakings and employment protection
applicable_laws: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 - Section 25N (Transfer of undertaking)
Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Breach of retention agreement
judgment: The court ruled in favor of the employees, holding that: 1) Retention agreements are enforceable contracts, 2) Termination within retention period without cause triggers full bonus payment, 3) The restructuring was designed to avoid retention obligations, amounting to fraud, 4) Employees entitled to full retention bonus plus severance. The court ordered: a) Payment of full retention bonuses to all terminated employees, b) Severance pay of 3 months salary, c) Accelerated vesting of all unvested stock options.
key_principles: Retention agreements are binding contractual obligations
Early termination within retention period triggers full payment
Change of control cannot be used to avoid employee obligations
Transfer of undertaking protects employee rights
Employees are not mere assets in M&A transactions
Constructive dismissal principles apply in post-acquisition changes
precedents: Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1997)
Buckingham and Carnatic Co. Ltd. v. Workers of the Company (1952)
Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India (2019) - Business transfer
practical_advice: Understand your rights in company acquisitions
Review and negotiate retention agreements carefully
Retention bonuses should have clear payment triggers
Document all promises made during acquisition process
Change of control clauses protect employee interests
Understand difference between stock deal and asset deal
Consult with lawyer before signing acquisition-related documents
Join employee groups to collectively negotiate better terms
Track vesting schedules during M&A transitions

case_name: Software Licensing and Open Source Compliance
scenario: A software company was sued for violating GPL license by incorporating open-source code into their proprietary product without releasing source code.
facts: The company used several open-source libraries with GPL v3 license in their commercial product. The product was sold as proprietary software without source code disclosure. Open-source community discovered the violation and initiated legal action.
legal_issues: Open source license compliance and violations
Commercial use of open source software
applicable_laws: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - License as contract
judgment: The court ruled in favor of the open-source copyright holders. Key findings: 1) GPL license is a valid and enforceable contract, 2) Use of GPL-licensed code in proprietary software without disclosure is copyright infringement, 3) Violation of copyleft provision requires disclosure of entire derivative work, 4) Company's claim of 'accidental inclusion' rejected due to negligence. The court ordered: a) Immediate release of full source code under GPL v3, b) Monetary damages for past violations, c) Permanent injunction against further violations.
key_principles: Open source licenses are legally enforceable contracts
GPL copyleft requires release of derivative works under GPL
Linking and incorporating GPL code creates derivative work
Ignorance of license terms is not a valid defense
Companies must have open source compliance policies
Violation can result in forced open-sourcing of entire product
precedents: Burlington Home Shopping Pvt. Ltd. v. Rajnish Chibber (1995) - Software copyright
Microsoft Corporation v. Yogesh Popat (2005) - License enforcement
Telemecanique & Controls (I) Pvt. Ltd. v. Schneider Electric Industries (2007)
practical_advice: Implement strict open source compliance policies
Maintain software bill of materials (SBOM) for all dependencies
Understand different open source licenses: GPL, MIT, Apache, BSD
GPL is copyleft - requires source disclosure for derivatives
Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache) allow proprietary use
Use license scanning tools to detect GPL code
Train developers on license compliance
Consider LGPL or linking exceptions for libraries
Document all third-party software and licenses
Consult IP lawyer for complex licensing scenarios
